title: Don't you want to be forgiven?
hookLine: Abu Bakr forgives a relative who spread the slander after this verse: pardon and overlook (24:22)

lines: ABU BAKR SUPPORTED MISTAH FOR YEARS.
cards: Three days ago, the rumor about 'A'isha. Now the other side of it. Her father, Abu Bakr, had a poor relative named Mistah, a cousin's son, and for years Abu Bakr had paid for his keep.

When the slander spread, Mistah was one of the people repeating it, about his own benefactor's daughter. After the verses came down clearing her, Abu Bakr swore an oath: he would never spend on Mistah again.
Plenty of people would call that fair. Then another verse came down.

teach.b: Verse twenty-two speaks to people of means who swear not to give to their relatives, the poor, and those who emigrated for God's sake. Mistah was all three.
Then, in Pickthall's words: "Let them forgive and show indulgence. Yearn ye not that Allah may forgive you?" Two verbs again.
Ya'fu: to pardon, to let the debt go. Yasfahu: to overlook, to turn away from it, to stop bringing it up.
Scholars often describe the second as one step further than the first: not only letting the wrong go, but not holding it over the person afterward. And then the question.

teach.h: DON'T YOU WANT TO BE FORGIVEN?
teach.b: Not a command, a question: don't you want God to forgive you? 'A'isha's account in Bukhari says that when Abu Bakr heard this, he said: yes, by God, I want God to forgive me.
He went back to supporting Mistah, and said he would never stop. Look at what the verse doesn't say. It doesn't say Mistah was right.
It doesn't say the harm was small; the verses before called it great. It doesn't ask Abu Bakr to trust Mistah with secrets.

teach.h: YES, BY GOD. THE SUPPORT RESUMES.
teach.b: It asks him not to cut off the support that kept a poor relative fed. Pardon isn't pretending it didn't happen, and it isn't letting someone keep hurting you.
It's refusing to make the rest of the relationship pay for one wound. And the reason it gives is personal: everyone needs forgiving for something.

how: Muslim teachers often tell the story of Abu Bakr and Mistah with 24:22 when speaking about forgiveness within families, and many Muslims recall its question when they find it hard to let go of a grievance.

o: the poor relative Abu Bakr kept supporting anyway
a relative who paid for Abu Bakr's keep for years
the man who found 'A'isha and led her camel home

games.q: inside the story — tap the pairs.

s: the verse says Mistah did nothing wrong
the verses before call the slander great in God's sight. 24:22 asks for pardon anyway.
Abu Bakr resumed supporting Mistah after the verse
he said, yes, by God, I want God to forgive me, and returned to supporting him.
pardon in this verse means trusting the person exactly as before
it asks not to cut off his support. it doesn't ask Abu Bakr to pretend nothing happened.

games.q: you're Abu Bakr. you've sworn never to support Mistah again. then you hear: don't you want God to forgive you? what do you do?
o: keep the oath; it was sworn before God.
say yes, by God, and go back to supporting him.
support him, but quietly tell people what he did.
games.why: he said yes, by God, I want God to forgive me, and resumed supporting Mistah, saying he would never stop.

practice: Think of someone who hurt you in a modest way, a careless word, a broken promise, a snub; not the deepest wound, and not anyone who is still harming you.
Notice what you've been holding back from them because of it, and ask yourself the verse's question, gently. If you pray, you can ask to be able to let it go, and to be forgiven too.

wordCard.voice: Mistah. The poor relative who spread the rumor about 'A'isha, and whom Abu Bakr chose to keep supporting anyway. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: let them pardon and let them overlook, from 24:22.

carryVoice: Your line: pardon, and be pardoned. Pardon never means letting someone keep hurting you. Day four hundred ninety-six, done.

sources.q: Let them forgive and show indulgence. Yearn ye not that Allah may forgive you?
